answer:
Evidence supports the claim:

- At BrightPath, scanned image-only PDFs made up about 60% of clinical documentation, and for those files citation mapping still failed, either pointing to page one of a 200-page document or generating no citation link; e.g., a code blue query answered correctly but cited page 1 of a 150-page document instead of page 87 [NL-018#NL-018-S04].
- Support data from May 2026: roughly 40–50% of ingested enterprise files were scanned PDFs without an embedded text layer; TutorChat either returned answers with no source citations because it could not find text offsets, or cited the whole document, e.g., page 1 of a 250-page PDF [NL-021#NL-021-S02].
- A monthly audit found that remaining citation tickets in May and June were almost entirely linked to scanned, image-only PDFs, where TutorChat struggled to establish citation anchors and often linked to the start of the file rather than the specific page [NL-011#NL-011-S05].
- KnowledgeHub guidance states scanned PDFs require OCR; without OCR they cannot be searched and citations cannot be generated, and OCR issues (blurry/low-res/handwriting/complex layouts) directly cause broken citations [NL-006#NL-006-S03]. Low-resolution scanned PDFs were also identified as a common root cause of "No citation available" because the layout parser could not determine the exact page or section ID [NL-006#NL-006-S04].
- The proposed upload warning explicitly says ingesting scanned/image-only files without OCR "may result in poor citation quality," and an example admin dashboard shows a scanned PDF detected at 45% Citation Confidence [NL-021#NL-021-S05].
- General documentation also states that low-quality scanned PDFs may cause the system to struggle to generate page-specific citations due to OCR limitations [NL-028#NL-028-S03].
